title: Who Experiences School Pressure at the Most Toxic Levels
author: Peter Gray
summary: Peter Gray discusses a Lancet Child and Adolescent Health study (Guo et al., 2026) that followed 4,714 UK adolescents and linked academic pressure at age 15 to depression and self-harm through age 24, even after controlling for many confounders. He treats this as another piece of evidence that school pressure is a causal contributor to youth mental health problems. His own contribution is a reading of the study's demographic table: girls were 25 percent more likely than boys to fall in the highest-pressure tertile, and students with top grades were 56 percent more likely than low-grade students. The largest effect was parental education, with students whose mothers held a post-secondary degree 139 percent more likely to be in the top tertile. Gray argues that school is a source of chronic rather than acute stress, which is not toughening, and that the pressure is preventable, citing his earlier letters and book on how schools can reduce it.
points: A large longitudinal UK study found academic pressure at 15 predicted depression and self-harm into the early twenties, even with confounders controlled.
Girls and students with high grades experience more academic pressure, suggesting a mental-health cost to school success.
Maternal education was the strongest predictor of pressure, consistent with research showing higher anxiety and depression in affluent, high-achieving families.
Chronic school stress differs from acute stress and does not build resilience the way short, surmountable challenges can.
Researchers describe academic pressure as a preventable cause of poor youth mental health, and schools have no excuse for ignoring it.
quotes: Even when controlling for all these variables, the researchers found a highly significant and rather substantial relationship between the level of school pressure experienced and subsequent levels of depression and likelihood of self-harm.

The researchers assessed level of school pressure, for 4714 adolescents, at age 15, using a questionnaire in which the teens rated the degree to which they (a) worried about getting their schoolwork done, (b) felt pressure from home to do well in school, and (c) believed it was important to score well on school tests.
Girls, on average, perform better than boys in school, but, apparently, at the cost of greater psychological damage.
So, academic pressure apparently correlates positively with good grades but negatively with mental health. Not a very satisfying tradeoff.

Those whose mother had a degree beyond high school were 139% more likely to be in the top tertile of school pressure than those whose mother’s highest level of schooling was a “certificate of secondary education.
But it is not true of chronic stress—the kind of stress that goes on day after day, month after month, year after year.
We have no excuse for allowing school, which children are required by law to attend, to be a major cause of psychological distress.
